extracted.intended_audience: graduate students applying for NIH F31 NRSA fellowships
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for deciding whether to revise and resubmit an NIH F31 NRSA fellowship application and how to prepare the resubmission, including reading summary statements, consulting program officers, and writing the Introduction to Application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application discussion status (Not Discussed vs Impact Score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review committees only discuss the top 50% of applications; half of applications receive a “Not Discussed” rather than a score. The other 50% receive an Impact Score and a percentile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not Discussed doesn’t mean your application has no chance for resubmission, but it does mean that it has a long way to go if you decide to revise and resubmit. Use posted paylines from Institutes cautiously—paylines vary by institute, mission alignment, and current funding climate; scores fundable in the past may not be fundable now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't contact Program Officer based only on score
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not immediately contact your Program Officer asking if your score is high enough to get funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program Officers can provide little information with just the score and will likely recommend waiting until you’ve received your summary statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate and read your Summary Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: After scoring, the summary statement (summary critiques from reviewers) will be posted in eRA Commons under the 'Other Relevant Documents' box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may take varying lengths of time to post (example: 2–4 weeks). You won't receive an email; check eRA Commons. Read it once to get a sense, then read again after emotions settle, carefully taking note of concerns and referring back to your application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess level and fixability of critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether reviewer criticisms are easily addressed with a revision or are more fundamental and hard to overcome in the same application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Not including enough experimental detail in the research strategy can usually be fixed; concerns about lack of training potential or impact are harder to overcome. Determine which critiques are surface-level (revisable) vs fundamental (may require major overhaul or different approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsor/mentor track record and training potential
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH values sponsors with a strong track record of mentoring predoctoral students and funding in the proposal's research area; lack of sponsor experience can hurt F31 proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sponsor is a new investigator, consider adding a more senior faculty co-sponsor and a letter of support to demonstrate training support and a collaborative environment—this can address concerns about training potential and mentoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact Program Officer to interpret summary statement and discuss resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Email the Program Officer to request a phone meeting after reviewing your summary statement to discuss the potential to resubmit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program Officers can interpret critiques, provide insights (e.g., whether reviewers were excited), and inform you if your application landed with the best Study Section; they may know additional context from attending review meetings that applicants lack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider study section assignment and potential reassignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether your application was reviewed by the best study section for your field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A review committee unfamiliar with your research may not appropriately assess your science; if appropriate, discuss moving to a different Study Section with your Program Officer to improve chances on resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider timeline and opportunity costs of resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor in submission cycles and project start dates when deciding to resubmit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resubmission means missing the next cycle (resubmission goes into a later cycle) and, even if funded, earliest project start date will be several months after the submission deadline. Discuss timelines with your thesis committee and Program Officer before deciding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start revising promptly and target largest weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin revision as soon as you review your summary statement and prioritize addressing the critiques that reviewers identified as the largest weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisory Council decisions take months, so prepare for likely resubmission. Work with your Program Officer (who may accept your rebuttals) and devise a revision strategy focused on major weaknesses rather than minor edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 'Introduction to Application' to respond to critiques respectfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Resubmissions must include an 'Introduction to Application' that responds to reviewer critiques; responses should be respectful and constructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the reviewers and thank them for their input. If you disagree with a critique, respond respectfully with a logical argument and references to support your reasoning. Tone matters—avoid dismissive or confrontational rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make clear what changes were made and make them easy to locate
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state what changes you made in the resubmission and make it easy for reviewers to find those changes in the application text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers will read your responses and check for your revisions—note where changes were made (and where) so reviewers can quickly verify revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add new information appropriately but don't rely on unrelated changes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to introduce changes beyond reviewer suggestions, but such changes should strengthen the application and not be expected to compensate for other critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you add material that doesn’t address a specific concern, don’t count on it to make up for unresolved critiques. In your response, note what updates you made, where they are, and how they strengthen the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace criticism and avoid rushing the resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reviewer criticism to build a stronger application and take time to prepare a high-quality resubmission rather than rushing to meet the next deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You only have one chance to resubmit (per summary statement cycle), so if rushing would compromise quality, it may be better to wait for a stronger revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to resubmitting the same application
rubrics_metrics.description: If you decide not to resubmit, other productive options exist, such as reworking the proposal as a new submission or applying to private grant foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overhaul specific aims if pursuing a new application and familiarize yourself with differences between a new submission and a resubmission. Treat the experience as learning—grant preparation itself is valuable professional development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary statement content and reviewer comment variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary statements contain reviewer critiques; the number and completeness of comments can vary across reviewers and criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from author's experience: each of three reviewers provided a summary critique, though only two provided additional comments on each criteria. Expect variability and read carefully to capture all actionable feedback.
